claim: Caveolae are small membrane pits with fundamental roles in mechanotransduction.
source: Caveolae are small membrane pits with fundamental roles in mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Caveolae flatten out in response to increased membrane tension.
source: Several studies have shown that caveolae flatten out in response to increased membrane tension, thereby acting as a mechanosensitive membrane reservoir that buffers acute mechanical stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies mentioned in the abstract.

claim: Caveolae act as a mechanosensitive membrane reservoir that buffers acute mechanical stress.
source: Several studies have shown that caveolae flatten out in response to increased membrane tension, thereby acting as a mechanosensitive membrane reservoir that buffers acute mechanical stress.
evidence: This is supported by references to several studies in the literature.

claim: Caveolae have been implicated in the control of RhoA/ROCK-mediated actomyosin contractility at the rear of migrating cells.
source: Caveolae have also been implicated in the control of RhoA/ROCK-mediated actomyosin contractility at the rear of migrating cells.
evidence: This statement references existing literature on caveolae function.

claim: Caveolae are highly enriched at the rear of migrating RPE1 cells.
source: Our data show that caveolae are highly enriched at the rear of migrating RPE1 cells and that membrane tension rapidly and reversibly disrupts the caveolar protein coat.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including microscopy and quantification.

claim: Membrane tension rapidly and reversibly disrupts the caveolar protein coat.
source: Our data show that caveolae are highly enriched at the rear of migrating RPE1 cells and that membrane tension rapidly and reversibly disrupts the caveolar protein coat.
evidence: This is supported by proximity proteomics and PLA data showing dissociation and reassociation of caveolar proteins.

claim: Membrane tension detaches caveolin-1 from focal adhesion proteins.
source: Membrane tension also detaches caveolin-1 from focal adhesion proteins and several mechanosensitive regulators of cortical actin including filamins and cortactin.
evidence: This is supported by proximity proteomics and PLA experiments showing reduced association under hypo-osmotic conditions.

claim: Membrane tension detaches caveolin-1 from filamins and cortactin.
source: Membrane tension also detaches caveolin-1 from focal adhesion proteins and several mechanosensitive regulators of cortical actin including filamins and cortactin.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data showing reduced signals under hypo-osmotic shock.

claim: ROCK associates with caveolin-1 in a manner dependent on membrane tension.
source: In addition, we present evidence that ROCK and the RhoGAP ARHGAP29 associate with caveolin-1 in a manner dependent on membrane tension, with ARHGAP29 influencing caveolin-1 Y14 phosphorylation, caveolae rear localisation, and RPE1 cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by proximity proteomics and PLA data showing enrichment under specific conditions.

claim: ARHGAP29 associates with caveolin-1 in a manner dependent on membrane tension.
source: In addition, we present evidence that ROCK and the RhoGAP ARHGAP29 associate with caveolin-1 in a manner dependent on membrane tension, with ARHGAP29 influencing caveolin-1 Y14 phosphorylation, caveolae rear localisation, and RPE1 cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by proximity proteomics showing ARHGAP29 enrichment in HYPO and REC samples.

claim: ARHGAP29 influences caveolin-1 Y14 phosphorylation.
source: In addition, we present evidence that ROCK and the RhoGAP ARHGAP29 associate with caveolin-1 in a manner dependent on membrane tension, with ARHGAP29 influencing caveolin-1 Y14 phosphorylation, caveolae rear localisation, and RPE1 cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing increased Cav1 Y14 phosphorylation upon ARHGAP29 knockdown.

claim: ARHGAP29 influences caveolae rear localisation.
source: In addition, we present evidence that ROCK and the RhoGAP ARHGAP29 associate with caveolin-1 in a manner dependent on membrane tension, with ARHGAP29 influencing caveolin-1 Y14 phosphorylation, caveolae rear localisation, and RPE1 cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing altered Cav1 distribution upon ARHGAP29 overexpression.

claim: ARHGAP29 influences RPE1 cell migration.
source: In addition, we present evidence that ROCK and the RhoGAP ARHGAP29 associate with caveolin-1 in a manner dependent on membrane tension, with ARHGAP29 influencing caveolin-1 Y14 phosphorylation, caveolae rear localisation, and RPE1 cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data showing reduced migration speed upon ARHGAP29 overexpression.

claim: Caveolae are composed of caveolin-1 and caveolin-2 embedded in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: They are composed of the scaffolding proteins caveolin-1 (Cav1) and caveolin-2 (Cav2), which are embedded in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, and the cavin protein family, which form a loose peripheral caveolar membrane coat.
evidence: This is established knowledge about caveolae structure.

claim: The cavin protein family forms a loose peripheral caveolar membrane coat.
source: They are composed of the scaffolding proteins caveolin-1 (Cav1) and caveolin-2 (Cav2), which are embedded in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, and the cavin protein family, which form a loose peripheral caveolar membrane coat.
evidence: This is established knowledge about caveolae structure.

claim: There are four cavins in humans: cavin1/PTRF, cavin2/SDPR, cavin3/SRBC, and cavin4/MURC.
source: There are four cavins in humans (cavin1/PTRF, cavin2/SDPR, cavin3/SRBC, and cavin4/MURC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cavin protein family.

claim: Cav1 and cavin1 are essential for caveolae formation.
source: Cav1 and cavin1 are essential for caveolae formation, whereas cavins 2–4 regulate caveolae dynamics and functions in a cell and tissue-specific fashion (Kovtun et al., 2015; Parton et al., 2020; Shvets et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cavins 2-4 regulate caveolae dynamics and functions in a cell and tissue-specific fashion.
source: Cav1 and cavin1 are essential for caveolae formation, whereas cavins 2–4 regulate caveolae dynamics and functions in a cell and tissue-specific fashion (Kovtun et al., 2015; Parton et al., 2020; Shvets et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EHD2 and Pacsin2 are localised to the caveolar neck.
source: While caveolins and cavins assemble into an oligomeric membrane coat that shapes the caveolar bulb (Gambin et al., 2014; Kovtun et al., 2015; Kovtun et al., 2014; Ludwig et al., 2013; Ludwig et al., 2016; Stoeber et al., 2016), EHD2 and Pacsin2 are localised to the caveolar neck and link caveolae to actin filaments to stabilise caveolae at the plasma membrane and to restrict their mobility (Hansen et al., 2011; Ludwig et al., 2013; Morén et al., 2012; Senju et al., 2011; Stoeber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EHD2 and Pacsin2 link caveolae to actin filaments to stabilise caveolae at the plasma membrane.
source: While caveolins and cavins assemble into an oligomeric membrane coat that shapes the caveolar bulb (Gambin et al., 2014; Kovtun et al., 2015; Kovtun et al., 2014; Ludwig et al., 2013; Ludwig et al., 2016; Stoeber et al., 2016), EHD2 and Pacsin2 are localised to the caveolar neck and link caveolae to actin filaments to stabilise caveolae at the plasma membrane and to restrict their mobility (Hansen et al., 2011; Ludwig et al., 2013; Morén et al., 2012; Senju et al., 2011; Stoeber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Caveolae are abundant in cells exposed to tensile forces or shear stress.
source: Caveolae are abundant in cells that are exposed to tensile forces or shear stress, such as endothelial cells, epithelial cells, and muscle cells, and protect such cells from mechanical stress (Chai et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2015; Dewulf et al., 2019; Garcia et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2017; Lo et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Caveolae protect cells from mechanical stress.
source: Caveolae are abundant in cells that are exposed to tensile forces or shear stress, such as endothelial cells, epithelial cells, and muscle cells, and protect such cells from mechanical stress (Chai et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2015; Dewulf et al., 2019; Garcia et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2017; Lo et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Caveolae disassemble in response to an increase in membrane tension.
source: There is evidence that caveolae disassemble (Sinha et al., 2011) or flatten out (Matthaeus et al., 2022) in response to an increase in membrane tension, and may similarly respond to other stresses such as osmotic stress (Guo et al., 2015), oxidative stress (Mougeolle et al., 2015), and UV irradiation (McMahon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tension-induced flattening is mediated by the dissociation of the peripheral cavin coat and EHD2 from membrane-embedded caveolin oligomers.
source: Tension-induced flattening was proposed to be mediated (or accompanied) by the dissociation of the peripheral cavin coat and EHD2 from membrane-embedded caveolin oligomers (Sinha et al., 2011; Yeow et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cavin complexes and EHD2 released into the cytosol can translocate into the nucleus to regulate gene transcription.
source: Cavin complexes and EHD2 released into the cytosol can subsequently translocate into the nucleus to regulate gene transcription (McMahon et al., 2021; McMahon et al., 2019; Torrino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Large numbers of caveolae are found at the rear of migrating cells.
source: Large numbers of caveolae are also found at the rear of migrating cells (Hetmanski et al., 2019; Ludwig et al., 2013), and several studies indicate an intricate relationship between caveolae-mediated mechanosensing and RhoA-mediated cell rear retraction (Grande-García and del Pozo, 2008; Grande-García et al., 2007; Hetmanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies including the authors' own work.

claim: Caveolae formation at the cell rear is promoted by low membrane tension.
source: Caveolae formation at the cell rear is promoted by low membrane tension and is dependent upon RhoA/ROCK1 signalling, the Rho guanidine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Ect2, and the RhoA effector protein and serine-threonine kinase PKN2 (Hetmanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Caveolae formation at the cell rear is dependent upon RhoA/ROCK1 signalling.
source: Caveolae formation at the cell rear is promoted by low membrane tension and is dependent upon RhoA/ROCK1 signalling, the Rho guanidine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Ect2, and the RhoA effector protein and serine-threonine kinase PKN2 (Hetmanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Caveolae enhance RhoA/ROCK1 signalling, leading to F-actin alignment, actomyosin contractility, and rapid rear retraction.
source: Caveolae, in turn, enhance RhoA/ROCK1 signalling, leading to F-actin alignment, actomyosin contractility, and rapid rear retraction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Loss of caveolae inhibits rear retraction and impedes cell migration.
source: Loss of caveolae, increased membrane tension, or inhibition of RhoA signalling all break this positive feedback loop, inhibiting rear retraction and impeding cell migration (Hetmanski et al., 2019; Hetmanski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A polarised rear distribution of Cav1 is observed in ~70% of RPE1 cells sparsely grown on fibronectin-coated glass.
source: Such a polarised rear distribution of Cav1 is observed in ~70% of RPE1 cells sparsely grown on fibronectin-coated glass.
evidence: This is based on quantification of fixed cell images.

claim: Cavin1-APEX2-EGFP is concentrated at the cell rear and colocalises with endogenous Cav1.
source: Cavin1-APEX2-EGFP (Cavin1-A2E) was concentrated at the cell rear and colocalised with endogenous Cav1, as expected (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and Pearson's correlation analysis shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: Cavin1 and cavin3 fusion proteins are stably associated with the cell rear for several hours in migrating RPE1 cells.
source: Time-lapse microscopy and quantitative tracking of caveolae localisation in RPE1 cells migrating on a fibronectin-coated glass surface showed that both cavin1 and cavin3 fusion proteins were stably associated with the cell rear for several hours (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—videos 1–3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Caveolae are associated with the rear of RPE1 cells migrating in a 3D collagen matrix.
source: Moreover, caveolae were associated with the rear of RPE1 cells migrating in a 3D collagen matrix (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Persistently migrating RPE1 cells show an average translocation rate of ~0.4 µm/min.
source: Persistently migrating RPE1 cells showed relatively uniform protrusion and retraction speeds, resulting in an average translocation rate of ~0.4 µm/min.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data.

claim: The migration speed of RPE1 cells is consistent with a previous report and comparable to cell migration speeds of MEFs, MDCK cells, and A2780 cells migrating in durotactic gradients.
source: This is consistent with a previous report (Vaidžiulytė et al., 2022) and comparable to cell migration speeds of MEFs and MDCK cells and A2780 cells migrating in durotactic gradients (Hetmanski et al., 2019; Sitarska and Diz-Muñoz, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rear retraction causes instantaneous and large cell rear displacements and an apparent accumulation of caveolae at the rear.
source: At a certain point, the rear suddenly retracted, causing instantaneous and large cell rear displacements and an apparent accumulation of caveolae at the rear (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and F).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: Caveolae rear localisation is rapidly re-established after cell division.
source: Similarly, caveolae rear localisation was rapidly re-established after cell division (Figure 1—video 8).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claim: When cells polarise spontaneously, caveolae become aligned along the long cell axis in a filament-like pattern.
source: Our live-cell imaging data further show that when cells polarise spontaneously, caveolae become aligned along the long cell axis in a filament-like pattern and eventually accumulate at the rear membrane as the rear retracts and the polarity axis is established (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—videos 9 and 10).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: 3D tomography reveals a dense network of surface-connected caveolae and large interconnected caveolar clusters at the cell rear.
source: 3D tomography and surface rendering of the tomograms revealed a dense network of surface-connected caveolae and the presence of large interconnected caveolar clusters, most of which appeared to be continuous with the rear plasma membrane (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cav1-A2E is expressed at levels comparable to or lower than that of endogenous Cav1 in RPE1 cells.
source: Cav1-A2E in RPE1 cells was expressed at levels comparable to or lower than that of endogenous Cav1 (Figure 3A), colocalised with PTRF/cavin1 at the cell rear (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and was stably associated with the rear in migrating cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cav1-A2E colocalises with PTRF/cavin1 at the cell rear.
source: Cav1-A2E in RPE1 cells was expressed at levels comparable to or lower than that of endogenous Cav1 (Figure 3A), colocalised with PTRF/cavin1 at the cell rear (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and was stably associated with the rear in migrating cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Cav1-A2E fusion protein is efficiently incorporated into caveolae.
source: Moreover, transmission electron microscopy showed that the Cav1-A2E fusion protein was efficiently incorporated into caveolae (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The biotinylation reaction in Cav1-A2E cells is dependent upon the presence of biotin phenol and hydrogen peroxide.
source: Streptavidin-HRP blotting of Cav1-A2E RPE1 cell lysates showed that the biotinylation reaction was dependent upon the presence of biotin phenol and a brief (1 min) exposure to hydrogen peroxide (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The biotinylation reaction is restricted to the cell rear and colocalises with Cav1-A2E.
source: In addition, fluorescent streptavidin labelling showed that the biotinylation reaction was restricted to the cell rear and colocalised with Cav1-A2E (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A total of 348 unique proteins were significantly enriched in the three Cav1 proximity proteomes after ratiometric filtering over the NES sample.
source: After ratiometric filtering over the NES sample, we identified a total of 348 unique proteins that were significantly enriched in the three Cav1 proximity proteomes (see Supplementary file 1 for the mass spectrometry data).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: 70 proteins were exclusive to the HYPO sample.
source: In total, 70 proteins were exclusive to the HYPO sample, 15 proteins were enriched specifically in the HYPO and REC samples, and 26 proteins were enriched specifically in the NT and REC samples (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 26 proteins were enriched specifically in the NT and REC samples.
source: In total, 70 proteins were exclusive to the HYPO sample, 15 proteins were enriched specifically in the HYPO and REC samples, and 26 proteins were enriched specifically in the NT and REC samples (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under hypo-osmotic conditions, Cav1, Cav2, and EHD2 were no longer significantly enriched with Cav1-A2E.
source: Importantly, Cav1-A2E and all major caveolar proteins (Cav1, Cav2, PTRF/cavin1, and EHD2; note that cavin2 and cavin3 are not expressed in RPE1 cells) were specifically enriched in the iso-osmotic control (NT) and recovered (REC) samples. On the contrary, under hypo-osmotic (HYPO) conditions, Cav1, Cav2, and EHD2 were no longer significantly enriched with Cav1-A2E (Figure 4C), suggesting that high membrane tension had caused the dissociation of these proteins from Cav1-A2E.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: High membrane tension causes the dissociation of Cav1, Cav2, and EHD2 from Cav1-A2E.
source: On the contrary, under hypo-osmotic (HYPO) conditions, Cav1, Cav2, and EHD2 were no longer significantly enriched with Cav1-A2E (Figure 4C), suggesting that high membrane tension had caused the dissociation of these proteins from Cav1-A2E.
evidence: This is inferred from the mass spectrometry data showing reduced enrichment under hypo-osmotic conditions.

claim: Cav1-A2E, PTRF/cavin1, and EHD2 were all specifically enriched in the NT and REC samples when directly compared to the HYPO sample.
source: Indeed, Cav1-A2E, PTRF/cavin1, and EHD2 were all specifically enriched in the NT and REC samples when directly compared to the HYPO sample (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No significant differences in the abundance of caveolar core components were observed between NT and REC samples.
source: By contrast, no significant differences in the abundance of caveolar core components were observed between NT and REC samples, suggesting that caveolae formation is fully restored within 30 min of recovery from a hypo-osmotic shock.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: Caveolae formation is fully restored within 30 min of recovery from a hypo-osmotic shock.
source: By contrast, no significant differences in the abundance of caveolar core components were observed between NT and REC samples, suggesting that caveolae formation is fully restored within 30 min of recovery from a hypo-osmotic shock.
evidence: This is inferred from the mass spectrometry data showing similar enrichment in NT and REC samples.

claim: The Cav1 proximity proteome is enriched in components of the cortical actin cytoskeleton and integrin adhesions.
source: Quantification of the MS data and GO annotation analyses revealed that the Cav1 proximity proteome was enriched in components of the cortical actin cytoskeleton and integrin adhesions, including filamins (FLNA, FLNB, FLNC), utrophin (UTRN), tensin-1 (TNS1), cortactin (CTTN), and paxillin (PXN) (Figure 4E and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on GO annotation analysis of the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4E and G.

claim: All caveolar proteins showed negative Z-scores under hypo-osmotic conditions.
source: Of note, all caveolar proteins showed negative Z-scores (i.e., were under-represented) under hypo-osmotic conditions (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on Z-score analysis of the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Pacsin2, utrophin, and tensin-1 were entirely absent from the Cav1 proximity proteome obtained in hypo-osmotic medium.
source: Some proteins such as Pacsin2, utrophin, and tensin-1 were entirely absent from the Cav1 proximity proteome obtained in hypo-osmotic medium (Figure 4E; indicated as NA).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Under iso-osmotic conditions, robust PLA signals were observed for Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1.
source: In agreement with our proteomics data, under iso-osmotic conditions we observed robust PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1, Cav1-A2E and filamin-A, and Cav1-A2E and cortactin (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Under iso-osmotic conditions, robust PLA signals were observed for Cav1-A2E and filamin-A.
source: In agreement with our proteomics data, under iso-osmotic conditions we observed robust PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1, Cav1-A2E and filamin-A, and Cav1-A2E and cortactin (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Under iso-osmotic conditions, robust PLA signals were observed for Cav1-A2E and cortactin.
source: In agreement with our proteomics data, under iso-osmotic conditions we observed robust PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1, Cav1-A2E and filamin-A, and Cav1-A2E and cortactin (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Robust PLA signals were observed for endogenous Cav1 and EHD2-A2E.
source: Moreover, robust signals were observed for endogenous Cav1 and an APEX2-EGFP fusion protein of EHD2 (EHD2-A2E) (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: 70-80% of the PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1 localised to the cell rear.
source: As expected, 70–80% of the PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1 and anti-Cav1 and EHD2-A2E localised to the cell rear, whilst rear-localised PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and filamin-A and Cav1-A2E and cortactin were significantly lower (~40%) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on quantification of PLA data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Rear-localised PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and filamin-A were approximately 40%.
source: As expected, 70–80% of the PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1 and anti-Cav1 and EHD2-A2E localised to the cell rear, whilst rear-localised PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and filamin-A and Cav1-A2E and cortactin were significantly lower (~40%) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on quantification of PLA data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Hypo-osmotic shock drastically reduced the PLA signals for Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1, Cav1-A2E and filamin-A, Cav1-A2E and cortactin, and Cav1 and EHD2-A2E.
source: Importantly, hypo-osmotic shock drastically reduced the PLA signals in all of the above cases, whereas cells that had recovered from the hypo-osmotic shock showed PLA signals indistinguishable to that of control cells.
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cells that had recovered from hypo-osmotic shock showed PLA signals indistinguishable from control cells.
source: Importantly, hypo-osmotic shock drastically reduced the PLA signals in all of the above cases, whereas cells that had recovered from the hypo-osmotic shock showed PLA signals indistinguishable to that of control cells.
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A brief hypo-osmotic shock causes an instantaneous but reversible disassembly of caveolae.
source: Taken together our data indicate that a brief hypo-osmotic shock causes an instantaneous but reversible disassembly of caveolae, as shown previously (Sinha et al., 2011; Torrino et al., 2018; Yeow et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the PLA and proteomics data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Membrane tension regulates the linkage between caveolae and the cortical actin cytoskeleton.
source: The data further imply that membrane tension regulates the linkage between caveolae and the cortical actin cytoskeleton and that caveolae assembly/disassembly is spatio-temporally coordinated with the reorganisation of the rear-localised actin cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the PLA and proteomics data showing tension-dependent changes in protein associations.

claim: Caveolae assembly/disassembly is spatio-temporally coordinated with the reorganisation of the rear-localised actin cortex.
source: The data further imply that membrane tension regulates the linkage between caveolae and the cortical actin cytoskeleton and that caveolae assembly/disassembly is spatio-temporally coordinated with the reorganisation of the rear-localised actin cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the live-cell imaging and PLA data.

claim: ROCK1 and HSPB1 were specifically enriched with Cav1 during the recovery phase.
source: Interestingly, several proteins were specifically enriched with Cav1 during the recovery phase (i.e., in HYPO and REC samples) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Among these proteins were Rho-associated protein kinase 1 (ROCK1) and the heat shock protein HSPB1.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rho/ROCK1 signalling is required for caveolae localisation to the rear of migrating cells.
source: Rho/ROCK1 signalling was previously shown to be required for caveolae localisation to the rear of migrating cells (Hetmanski et al., 2019) and HSPB1 is a stress-regulated actin binding protein implicated in mechanotransduction and cell migration (Clarke and Mearow, 2013; Collier et al., 2019; Hoffman et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HSPB1 is a stress-regulated actin binding protein implicated in mechanotransduction and cell migration.
source: Rho/ROCK1 signalling was previously shown to be required for caveolae localisation to the rear of migrating cells (Hetmanski et al., 2019) and HSPB1 is a stress-regulated actin binding protein implicated in mechanotransduction and cell migration (Clarke and Mearow, 2013; Collier et al., 2019; Hoffman et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The association of HSPB1 and ROCK1 with Cav1 is significantly enhanced in cells exposed to hypo-osmotic shock and in cells that had recovered from the shock.
source: PLAs confirmed that the association of both HSPB1 and ROCK1 with Cav1 is significantly enhanced in cells exposed to hypo-osmotic shock and in cells that had recovered from the shock (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: ROCK inhibition blocked caveolae rear localisation.
source: ROCK inhibition blocked caveolae rear localisation (Figure 5H and I) and significantly reduced the PLA signal between Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1, but did not affect the Cav1-A2E/filamin-A interaction (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5H-J.

claim: ROCK inhibition significantly reduced the PLA signal between Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1.
source: ROCK inhibition blocked caveolae rear localisation (Figure 5H and I) and significantly reduced the PLA signal between Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1, but did not affect the Cav1-A2E/filamin-A interaction (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: ROCK inhibition did not affect the Cav1-A2E/filamin-A interaction.
source: ROCK inhibition blocked caveolae rear localisation (Figure 5H and I) and significantly reduced the PLA signal between Cav1-A2E and PTRF/cavin1, but did not affect the Cav1-A2E/filamin-A interaction (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: PLA signals between Cav1-A2E and ROCK1 were significantly increased upon ROCK inhibition.
source: Interestingly, PLA signals between Cav1-A2E and ROCK1 as well as between Cav1-A2E and HSPB1 were significantly increased upon ROCK inhibition (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: PLA signals between Cav1-A2E and HSPB1 were significantly increased upon ROCK inhibition.
source: Interestingly, PLA signals between Cav1-A2E and ROCK1 as well as between Cav1-A2E and HSPB1 were significantly increased upon ROCK inhibition (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is based on PLA data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: ROCK1 and HSPB1 are recruited to caveolae at high membrane tension.
source: This corroborates our proximity proteomics data and suggests that (a) ROCK1 and HSPB1 are recruited to caveolae (or the cell rear) at high membrane tension, (b) that ROCK activity is required for caveolae reassembly after hypo-osmotic shock, and (c) that ROCK activity weakens the protein's association with caveolae (or the cell rear).
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics and PLA data.

claim: ROCK activity is required for caveolae reassembly after hypo-osmotic shock.
source: This corroborates our proximity proteomics data and suggests that (a) ROCK1 and HSPB1 are recruited to caveolae (or the cell rear) at high membrane tension, (b) that ROCK activity is required for caveolae reassembly after hypo-osmotic shock, and (c) that ROCK activity weakens the protein's association with caveolae (or the cell rear).
evidence: This is inferred from the PLA data showing reduced caveolae reassembly upon ROCK inhibition.

claim: ROCK activity weakens ROCK1 and HSPB1 association with caveolae.
source: This corroborates our proximity proteomics data and suggests that (a) ROCK1 and HSPB1 are recruited to caveolae (or the cell rear) at high membrane tension, (b) that ROCK activity is required for caveolae reassembly after hypo-osmotic shock, and (c) that ROCK activity weakens the protein's association with caveolae (or the cell rear).
evidence: This is inferred from the PLA data showing increased association upon ROCK inhibition.

claim: ARHGAP29 regulates mechanotransduction in a YAP-dependent manner.
source: One of these proteins, the RhoGAP ARHGAP29, has been shown to regulate mechanotransduction in a YAP-dependent manner and to control cancer cell migration and invasion by suppressing actin polymerisation through a Rho/LIMK/cofilin pathway (Meng et al., 2018; Qiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ARHGAP29 controls cancer cell migration and invasion by suppressing actin polymerisation through a Rho/LIMK/cofilin pathway.
source: One of these proteins, the RhoGAP ARHGAP29, has been shown to regulate mechanotransduction in a YAP-dependent manner and to control cancer cell migration and invasion by suppressing actin polymerisation through a Rho/LIMK/cofilin pathway (Meng et al., 2018; Qiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YAP regulates caveolar gene transcription and caveolae formation.
source: YAP also regulates caveolar gene transcription and caveolae formation (Rausch et al., 2019), and there is evidence that caveolae, in turn, regulate YAP (Moreno-Vicente et al., 2019; Rausch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Caveolae regulate YAP.
source: YAP also regulates caveolar gene transcription and caveolae formation (Rausch et al., 2019), and there is evidence that caveolae, in turn, regulate YAP (Moreno-Vicente et al., 2019; Rausch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ARHGAP29, YAP, and pS127 YAP levels were significantly increased in Cav1 siRNA cells.
source: Interestingly, ARHGAP29, YAP, and pS127 YAP levels (a common readout for HIPPO pathway activity) were significantly increased in Cav1 siRNA cells.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The levels of phosphorylated myosin light chain (pMLC) were markedly decreased in Cav1 siRNA cells.
source: In addition, the levels of phosphorylated myosin light chain (pMLC, a common readout for myosin-II activation) were markedly decreased in Cav1 siRNA cells.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: ARHGAP29 siRNA transfected cells showed a significant increase in Cav1 Y14 phosphorylation.
source: By contrast, ARHGAP29 siRNA transfected cells showed a significant increase in Cav1 Y14 phosphorylation, but pMLC levels were not significantly different to control cells.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: pMLC levels were not significantly different in ARHGAP29 siRNA cells compared to control cells.
source: By contrast, ARHGAP29 siRNA transfected cells showed a significant increase in Cav1 Y14 phosphorylation, but pMLC levels were not significantly different to control cells.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: YAP and YAP target gene expression as well as ARHGAP29 mRNA levels were unchanged in Cav1 knockdown cells.
source: YAP and YAP target gene expression [CYR61 (CCN1), CTGF (CCN2), ANKRD1] as well as ARHGAP29 mRNA levels were unchanged in Cav1 knockdown cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of A2E-ARHGAP29 perturbed the polarised rear distribution of Cav1.
source: Quantification of this phenotype revealed that overexpression of A2E-ARHGAP29 indeed perturbed the polarised rear distribution of Cav1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cells overexpressing A2E-ARHGAP29 established multiple random protrusions and failed to specify a stable front-rear axis.
source: By contrast, cells overexpressing A2E-ARHGAP29 established multiple random protrusions and failed to specify a stable front-rear axis, resulting either in a complete loss of cell motility (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—video 2) or in short migration tracks and frequent reversals in direction (Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: This is based on live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: ARHGAP29-overexpressing cells showed markedly reduced migration velocities compared to control-transfected cells.
source: Consequently, ARHGAP29-overexpressing cells showed markedly reduced migration velocities and mean squared displacements compared to control-transfected cells (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is based on quantification of live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: ARHGAP29-overexpressing cells showed markedly reduced mean squared displacements compared to control-transfected cells.
source: Consequently, ARHGAP29-overexpressing cells showed markedly reduced migration velocities and mean squared displacements compared to control-transfected cells (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is based on quantification of live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: ARHGAP29 negatively regulates caveolae rear localisation and RPE1 cell migration.
source: Taken together the data indicate that ARHGAP29 negatively regulates caveolae rear localisation and RPE1 cell migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence and live-cell imaging data showing altered caveolae distribution and reduced migration upon ARHGAP29 overexpression.

claim: The Cav1 interactome is enriched in proteins that are present at but not necessarily exclusive to the cell rear.
source: We note that the Cav1 interactome is enriched in proteins that are present at but not necessarily exclusive to the cell rear.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics data and immunofluorescence showing proteins like filamin-A and cortactin are not exclusively at the rear.

claim: The Cav1 interactome represents a composite cell-wide interactome of Cav1 oligomers and fully assembled caveolae.
source: Therefore, the Cav1 interactome is not a specific interactome of caveolae at the cell rear but rather represents a composite cell-wide interactome of Cav1 oligomers and fully assembled caveolae.
evidence: This is inferred from the understanding that Cav1-APEX2 is present throughout the cell.

claim: The entire caveolar coat structure is re-established within 30 min of recovery from hypo-osmotic shock.
source: The data also revealed that the entire caveolar coat structure is re-established within 30 min of recovery from the shock, demonstrating that caveolae assembly and disassembly are remarkably dynamic.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics and PLA data showing similar enrichment in NT and REC samples.

claim: Caveolae assembly and disassembly are remarkably dynamic.
source: The data also revealed that the entire caveolar coat structure is re-established within 30 min of recovery from the shock, demonstrating that caveolae assembly and disassembly are remarkably dynamic.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid changes observed in the proteomics and PLA data.

claim: Flat Cav1 scaffolds contain detectable levels of cavins.
source: It is worth noting that flat Cav1 scaffolds have recently been shown to contain detectable levels of cavins and that EHD2 and Pacsin2 are associated both with flat and curved caveolae (Matthaeus et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: EHD2 and Pacsin2 are associated both with flat and curved caveolae.
source: It is worth noting that flat Cav1 scaffolds have recently been shown to contain detectable levels of cavins and that EHD2 and Pacsin2 are associated both with flat and curved caveolae (Matthaeus et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Membrane tension either dissociates the caveolar coat partially or induces a substantial structural remodelling of many but not all caveolae.
source: Nonetheless, our work clearly shows that membrane tension has a profound effect on caveolae and that such changes are quantifiable. Altogether, we suggest that membrane tension either dissociates the caveolar coat partially or induces a substantial structural remodelling of many but not all caveolae.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics and PLA data showing partial dissociation of caveolar proteins.

claim: Large clusters of morphologically distinct caveolae and interconnected caveolar networks were observed at the RPE1 cell rear using electron tomography.
source: Although we cannot discriminate between flat and invaginated caveolae at the resolution provided by diffraction-limited microscopy, large clusters of morphologically distinct caveolae and interconnected caveolar networks were observed at the RPE1 cell rear using electron tomography.
evidence: This is based on electron tomography data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A polarised distribution of caveolae has been demonstrated in many other migratory cell types.
source: Such a polarised distribution of caveolae has been demonstrated in many other migratory cell types (Grande-García and del Pozo, 2008; Grande-García et al., 2007; Hetmanski et al., 2019; Joshi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Low membrane tension favours caveolae formation.
source: Several studies have shown that low membrane tension favours caveolae formation (Del Pozo et al., 2021; Golani et al., 2019; Sinha et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The formation of caveolae specifically at the rear of migrating cells is the result of a relatively stable front-rear asymmetry in membrane tension.
source: This suggests that the formation of caveolae specifically at the rear of migrating cells is the result of a relatively stable front-rear asymmetry in membrane tension.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that low tension favours caveolae formation and caveolae are enriched at the rear.

claim: Membrane tension gradients with low tension at the rear and higher tension at the front have been observed in fast-moving fish keratocytes.
source: Such membrane tension gradients, with low tension at the rear and higher tension at the front, have indeed been observed in fast-moving fish keratocytes (Lieber et al., 2015; Lieber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stable front-rear membrane tension gradients exist in many migrating cells, including RPE1 cells.
source: Using fluorescence lifetime imaging with the Flipper-TR membrane tension probe, the Roux lab recently reported that stable front-rear membrane tension gradients indeed exist in many migrating cells, including RPE1 cells (García-Arcos et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Tension gradients were observed in non-migrating cells and were dependent upon a dynamic F-actin network, cell–substrate adhesions, and membrane–cortex attachments.
source: Tension gradients were even observed in non-migrating cells and were dependent upon a dynamic F-actin network, cell–substrate adhesions, and membrane–cortex attachments.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: A2780 cells exhibit a front/rear membrane tension gradient only when cells migrate in an ECM rigidity gradient.
source: Hetmanski et al. reported that A2780 cells exhibit a front/rear membrane tension gradient only when cells migrate in an ECM rigidity gradient (Hetmanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Inhibition of Rho signalling by Y-27632 increased rear membrane tension and prevented the accumulation of cavin1 and Cav1 at the rear.
source: Both inhibition of Rho signalling by Y-27632 and expression of a constitutively active ezrin mutant (which enhances membrane–cortex interactions at the cell rear) increased rear membrane tension, prevented the accumulation of cavin1 and Cav1 at the rear, and blocked cell rear retraction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Expression of a constitutively active ezrin mutant increased rear membrane tension and prevented the accumulation of cavin1 and Cav1 at the rear.
source: Both inhibition of Rho signalling by Y-27632 and expression of a constitutively active ezrin mutant (which enhances membrane–cortex interactions at the cell rear) increased rear membrane tension, prevented the accumulation of cavin1 and Cav1 at the rear, and blocked cell rear retraction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Caveolae become concentrated at the rear when cells retract their trailing edge.
source: The role of contractility in concentrating caveolae at the rear is also evident in our time-lapse movies, which suggest that caveolae (cavins) become concentrated at the rear when cells retract their trailing edge.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Sudden rear retractions are likely the result of bursts of contractility that pull on the rear membrane, lowering tension at the rear and promoting caveolae formation.
source: Such sudden rear retractions are likely the result of bursts of contractility that pull on the rear membrane, lowering tension at the rear and promoting caveolae formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-lapse imaging data and knowledge of how contractility affects membrane tension.

claim: Caveolae are attached to and aligned along actin filaments.
source: Caveolae are indeed attached to and aligned along actin filaments (Echarri and Del Pozo, 2015; Richter et al., 2008; Stoeber et al., 2012) and depolymerisation of the actin cytoskeleton or inhibition of actomyosin contractility affects caveolae distribution and dynamics (Hetmanski et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2021) and blocks caveolae rear localisation (Hetmanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depolymerisation of the actin cytoskeleton or inhibition of actomyosin contractility affects caveolae distribution and dynamics.
source: Caveolae are indeed attached to and aligned along actin filaments (Echarri and Del Pozo, 2015; Richter et al., 2008; Stoeber et al., 2012) and depolymerisation of the actin cytoskeleton or inhibition of actomyosin contractility affects caveolae distribution and dynamics (Hetmanski et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2021) and blocks caveolae rear localisation (Hetmanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Actomyosin-driven contraction and a front/rear membrane tension gradient promote caveolae formation specifically at the rear.
source: Altogether our data and a large body of existing literature indicate that caveolae are associated with the F-actin cytoskeleton and that actomyosin-driven contraction and a front/rear membrane tension gradient promote caveolae formation specifically at the rear.
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A stable membrane tension gradient exists in RPE1 cells.
source: The model assumes that a stable membrane tension gradient exists in RPE1 cells (García-Arcos et al., 2024), promoting caveolae formation at the rear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Protrusion at the front is coupled to retraction at the rear.
source: Considering evidence that protrusion at the front is coupled to retraction at the rear and that membrane tension can propagate across the cell (De Belly et al., 2023; Houk et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2017; Sitarska and Diz-Muñoz, 2020; Tsai et al., 2019), it can be inferred that at short time scales absolute membrane tension values fluctuate at both the rear and the front.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Membrane tension can propagate across the cell.
source: Considering evidence that protrusion at the front is coupled to retraction at the rear and that membrane tension can propagate across the cell (De Belly et al., 2023; Houk et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2017; Sitarska and Diz-Muñoz, 2020; Tsai et al., 2019), it can be inferred that at short time scales absolute membrane tension values fluctuate at both the rear and the front.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At short time scales absolute membrane tension values fluctuate at both the rear and the front.
source: Considering evidence that protrusion at the front is coupled to retraction at the rear and that membrane tension can propagate across the cell (De Belly et al., 2023; Houk et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2017; Sitarska and Diz-Muñoz, 2020; Tsai et al., 2019), it can be inferred that at short time scales absolute membrane tension values fluctuate at both the rear and the front.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about tension propagation and front-rear coupling.

claim: Caveolae assembly and disassembly at the rear is coordinated with or driven by the protrusion/retraction cycle.
source: This would suggest that caveolae assembly and disassembly at the rear is coordinated with or driven by the protrusion/retraction cycle: When rear tension drops (e.g. in response to a sudden rear retraction), the formation of caveolae and caveolar networks is favoured. When tension at the rear builds up (e.g. when front protrusion is dominant over rear retraction), caveolae flatten out.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-lapse imaging data and the understanding of how tension affects caveolae.

claim: When rear tension drops, the formation of caveolae and caveolar networks is favoured.
source: This would suggest that caveolae assembly and disassembly at the rear is coordinated with or driven by the protrusion/retraction cycle: When rear tension drops (e.g. in response to a sudden rear retraction), the formation of caveolae and caveolar networks is favoured.
evidence: This is inferred from the understanding that low tension favours caveolae formation.

claim: When tension at the rear builds up, caveolae flatten out.
source: When tension at the rear builds up (e.g. when front protrusion is dominant over rear retraction), caveolae flatten out.
evidence: This is inferred from the understanding that high tension causes caveolae flattening.

claim: Caveolae and caveolar networks substantially increase the effective membrane surface.
source: Since caveolae and caveolar networks substantially increase the effective membrane surface (Golani et al., 2019) and also provide a unique topology and curvature, their dynamic and reversible nature might not only be critical for buffering membrane tension, but also play an important role in regulating the recruitment of signalling proteins to the rear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The dynamic and reversible nature of caveolae might play an important role in regulating the recruitment of signalling proteins to the rear.
source: Since caveolae and caveolar networks substantially increase the effective membrane surface (Golani et al., 2019) and also provide a unique topology and curvature, their dynamic and reversible nature might not only be critical for buffering membrane tension, but also play an important role in regulating the recruitment of signalling proteins to the rear.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the properties of caveolae.

claim: Knockdown of RhoA, ROCK1, or the rear-localised RhoGEF Ect2 in A2780 cells blocked caveolae rear localisation and impeded cell migration in durotactic gradients.
source: Knockdown of RhoA, ROCK1, or the rear-localised RhoGEF Ect2 in A2780 cells blocked caveolae rear localisation and impeded cell migration in durotactic gradients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Caveolae were required for the recruitment of Ect2 to the rear, for RhoA activation, and for cell rear retraction.
source: Caveolae, in turn, were required for the recruitment of Ect2 to the rear, for RhoA activation, and for cell rear retraction, suggesting that caveolae and the actomyosin system control cell rear retraction via a positive feedback loop (Hetmanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Caveolae and the actomyosin system control cell rear retraction via a positive feedback loop.
source: Caveolae, in turn, were required for the recruitment of Ect2 to the rear, for RhoA activation, and for cell rear retraction, suggesting that caveolae and the actomyosin system control cell rear retraction via a positive feedback loop (Hetmanski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The loss of Cav1 leads to a drastic reduction in MLC phosphorylation.
source: In addition, we show that the loss of Cav1 leads to a drastic reduction in MLC phosphorylation, indicating that Cav1 is critical for myosin-II activation.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Cav1 is critical for myosin-II activation.
source: In addition, we show that the loss of Cav1 leads to a drastic reduction in MLC phosphorylation, indicating that Cav1 is critical for myosin-II activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the western blot data showing reduced pMLC upon Cav1 knockdown.

claim: Cav1 scaffolds recruit Ect2 and ROCK1 to the cell rear to promote caveolae formation and actomyosin contractility.
source: Altogether this suggests that Cav1 scaffolds recruit Ect2 and ROCK1 to the cell rear to promote caveolae formation and actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and previous studies.

claim: The function of ARHGAP29 might be to interrupt the positive feedback loop between caveolae and actomyosin by suppressing RhoA signalling at the rear.
source: As discussed below, the function of ARHGAP29 might be to interrupt this feedback loop by suppressing RhoA signalling at the rear.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the data.

claim: ARHGAP29 is localised to the plasma membrane in several cell types.
source: This was somewhat unexpected as ARHGAP29 is localised to the plasma membrane in several cell types (Post et al., 2015; Rogg et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2020b; Tan and Zaidel-Bar, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A fraction of ARHGAP29 was present in lamellipodia-like protrusions, which were largely devoid of Cav1.
source: Closer inspection revealed that a fraction of ARHGAP29 was present in lamellipodia-like protrusions, which interestingly were largely devoid of Cav1.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data.

claim: ARHGAP29 can locally suppress caveolae assembly or prevent caveolae recruitment into lamellipodia-like protrusions.
source: This inverse spatial correlation suggests that ARHGAP29 can locally suppress caveolae assembly or prevent caveolae recruitment into such areas.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing inverse correlation.

claim: The effect of ARHGAP29 on caveolae is likely due to the local inhibition of RhoA.
source: This effect is likely due to the local inhibition of RhoA and can explain the caveolae rear polarity and cell migration defects we observe in cells overexpressing ARHGAP29.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of ARHGAP29 as a RhoGAP.

claim: Within 1 min time frame, ARHGAP29 cycles on and off the rear membrane (kiss and run).
source: It is conceivable, therefore, that within this 1 min time frame, ARHGAP29 cycles on and off the rear membrane (kiss and run).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain the proteomics data.

claim: ARHGAP29 contains an N-terminal F-BAR domain that is required for membrane targeting and that can sense changes in membrane curvature.
source: Interestingly, ARHGAP29 contains an N-terminal F-BAR domain that is required for membrane targeting and that can sense changes in membrane curvature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ARHGAP29 structure and function.

claim: Membrane recruitment of SPV-1, the worm orthologue of ARHGAP29, is favoured at low membrane tension, leading to RhoA inactivation at the cortex.
source: Work in Caenorhabditis elegans suggests that membrane recruitment of SPV-1, the worm orthologue of ARHGAP29, is favoured at low membrane tension, leading to RhoA inactivation at the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Increased membrane tension releases ARHGAP29 from the membrane, permitting cortical RhoA activation and contractility.
source: Increased membrane tension releases ARHGAP29 from the membrane, permitting cortical RhoA activation and contractility (Tan and Zaidel-Bar, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Subtle changes in membrane tension might control ARHGAP29 levels at the cell rear.
source: This is line with our proteomics data and suggests that subtle changes in membrane tension might control ARHGAP29 levels at the cell rear.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics data and the cited study on SPV-1.

claim: Recruitment of ARHGAP29 to the rear at low membrane tension would transiently suppress Rho-mediated contractility.
source: Recruitment of ARHGAP29 to the rear at low membrane tension (which presumably occurs immediately following the retraction of the rear) would transiently suppress Rho-mediated contractility, providing a potential mechanism to terminate rear retraction and to permit a new protrusion/retraction cycle.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the data and the known function of ARHGAP29.

claim: ARHGAP29 might be involved in establishing a Rac/Rho activity gradient along the front/rear axis.
source: Instead of transiently operating at the rear where RhoA-GTP levels are relatively high, it is equally possible that ARHGAP29 inhibits Rho activation at the cell front, similar to what has been suggested for podocytes (Rogg et al., 2023). In this scenario, ARHGAP29 might be involved in establishing a Rac/Rho activity gradient along the front/rear axis (Ridley et al., 2003) rather than dampening RhoA activity at the rear.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on alternative interpretations of the data.

claim: Cav1 and ARHGAP29 control actin dynamics in fundamentally different ways.
source: This suggests that Cav1 and ARHGAP29 control actin dynamics in fundamentally different ways.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on pMLC levels.

claim: Cav1 promotes cell rear retraction via RhoA/ROCK/MLC signalling.
source: Whilst Cav1 promotes cell rear retraction via RhoA/ROCK/MLC signalling (Hetmanski et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2021), ARHGAP29 may control the stability or turnover of F-actin networks by suppressing a RhoA/LIMK/cofilin pathway (Qiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ARHGAP29 may control the stability or turnover of F-actin networks by suppressing a RhoA/LIMK/cofilin pathway.
source: Whilst Cav1 promotes cell rear retraction via RhoA/ROCK/MLC signalling (Hetmanski et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2021), ARHGAP29 may control the stability or turnover of F-actin networks by suppressing a RhoA/LIMK/cofilin pathway (Qiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cofilin-driven actin depolymerisation plays an important role in cell motility.
source: Cofilin-driven actin depolymerisation plays an important role in cell motility (Bravo-Cordero et al., 2013), although there is conflicting data over whether cofilin is active at the leading edge (Bisaria et al., 2020) or at the cell rear (Mseka and Cramer, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin-II and cofilin crosstalk to control actomyosin dynamics.
source: Since myosin-II and cofilin crosstalk to control actomyosin dynamics (Wiggan et al., 2012), the functions of ARHGAP29 and caveolae may be intertwined in a complex manner.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and is speculative reasoning.

claim: Downregulation of ARHGAP29 significantly increases Cav1 Y14 phosphorylation.
source: Thirdly, we find that downregulation of ARHGAP29 significantly increases Cav1 Y14 phosphorylation, whilst downregulation of Cav1 stabilises or promotes the expression of ARHGAP29.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Downregulation of Cav1 stabilises or promotes the expression of ARHGAP29.
source: Thirdly, we find that downregulation of ARHGAP29 significantly increases Cav1 Y14 phosphorylation, whilst downregulation of Cav1 stabilises or promotes the expression of ARHGAP29.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Y14 phosphorylation is dependent upon ROCK and Src activity.
source: Previous studies have shown that Y14 phosphorylation is dependent upon ROCK and Src activity and a role in the control of focal adhesion dynamics, cell migration, and caveolae-mediated mechanosignalling has been proposed (Joshi et al., 2012; Joshi et al., 2008; Meng et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2021; Zimnicka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Y14 phosphorylation plays a role in the control of focal adhesion dynamics, cell migration, and caveolae-mediated mechanosignalling.
source: Previous studies have shown that Y14 phosphorylation is dependent upon ROCK and Src activity and a role in the control of focal adhesion dynamics, cell migration, and caveolae-mediated mechanosignalling has been proposed (Joshi et al., 2012; Joshi et al., 2008; Meng et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2021; Zimnicka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ARHGAP29 interferes with RhoA/ROCK or Src signalling to suppress Cav1 phosphorylation.
source: Taken together this suggests that ARHGAP29 interferes with RhoA/ROCK or Src signalling to suppress Cav1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased Cav1 Y14 phosphorylation upon ARHGAP29 knockdown.

claim: Caveolae dampen ARHGAP29 expression to reinforce a positive feedback loop that promotes actomyosin-mediated cell rear retraction.
source: Caveolae, in turn, somehow dampen ARHGAP29 expression to reinforce a positive feedback loop that promotes actomyosin-mediated cell rear retraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased ARHGAP29 upon Cav1 knockdown and is speculative reasoning.

claim: Caveolae act as a rear-localised membrane tension sensor that links the F-actin cortex and actomyosin contractility to cell rear retraction.
source: In conclusion, our data and previous work (Hetmanski et al., 2019; Hetmanski et al., 2021) suggest that caveolae act as a rear-localised membrane tension sensor that links the F-actin cortex and actomyosin contractility to cell rear retraction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented and previous studies.
